note: Published estimates of how much electricity US data centers use and will use. This is the demand half of the page's denominator, and it is a curated file rather than a computed one because no public dataset measures it: EIA meters the commercial sector, not the data-center subset of it, so every number in this table is somebody's estimate and is labelled with whose. Rules for adding a row, in order of importance. (1) One estimate, one row, from the report itself or its own summary page — never a news article's restatement when the report is reachable, and never a paywalled body. (2) `basis` is the field that keeps this table honest and is required. `level` means the row is a quantity in that year (LBNL's 176 TWh in 2023). `increment` means it is growth relative to a base year (the IEA's '+240 TWh by 2030'), and then `base_year` must say relative to what. `share` means it is a percentage of national consumption. Put a level and an increment in one column headed TWh with nothing to tell them apart and someone will add them together. (3) `scenario` is the report's own name for the case — 'low', 'high', 'base', 'Lift-Off' — not a word of ours. A report publishing a range becomes one row per case, never a midpoint. (4) `geography` is 'US' unless the figure is global or regional, in which case say which; a global figure quoted as if it were American is the most common error in this literature. (5) `caveat` is one or two sentences for a reader: what this number does not include. Crypto mining, on-site generation and transmission losses are in some of these estimates and not others, and that difference is larger than the spread between the estimates. Every row needs one. (6) `last_checked` is the day somebody last opened `source_url` and confirmed the figure still reads as recorded; after config.REFERENCE_STALE_DAYS days the page greys the row. (7) Never delete a superseded estimate — add the new one and let the page show how the published view moved. The 2023-vintage forecasts being wrong is itself a finding. Working notes go in `curator_notes`, which pipelines/power/reference.py strips before publishing.

rows.source_name: Berkeley Lab, "Berkeley Lab Report Evaluates Increase in Electricity Demand from Data Centers" (summary of the 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report)
rows.quote: climbed from 58 TWh in 2014 to 176 TWh in 2023
rows.caveat: Covers servers, storage, network equipment and cooling and power infrastructure inside US data centers, and excludes cryptocurrency mining, which Berkeley Lab estimates separately. It is electricity delivered to the site, so transmission and distribution losses upstream are not counted.
rows.curator_notes: The report body rounds 2014-2016 to "about 60 TWh" and does not print 58; the 58 TWh figure is stated in Berkeley Lab's own news summary of the report, which is the URL used here. Modelled bottom-up from equipment shipments, not metered.

rows.source_name: Shehabi et al., "2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report", LBNL-2001637
rows.quote: data centers consumed about 76 TWh, representing 1.9% of total
rows.caveat: Excludes cryptocurrency mining, which this report models separately in its own section. Includes on-site cooling and power infrastructure but not transmission and distribution losses, and not electricity generated on site.
rows.curator_notes: Bottom-up model from IT equipment shipment data plus modelled PUE; the report calls years before 2024 historical best estimates rather than forecasts.

rows.source_name: Shehabi et al., "2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report", LBNL-2001637
rows.quote: reaching 176 TWh by 2023, representing 4.4% of total U.S. electricity consumption
rows.caveat: Excludes cryptocurrency mining, which the report estimates separately, so it is not comparable with estimates such as EPRI's that fold mining in. Includes cooling and power infrastructure at the site; excludes grid losses.
rows.curator_notes: This is the single most quoted number in the literature and the anchor most later forecasts are indexed to. Same figure repeated in section 5.5 and the executive summary.

rows.source_name: Shehabi et al., "2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report", LBNL-2001637
rows.quote: the low and high end of roughly 325 and 580 TWh in 2028
rows.caveat: Excludes cryptocurrency mining and grid losses. The spread comes from assumptions about GPU shipments, how hard and how often AI servers run, and cooling system choice; it is not a probability range and the report attaches no likelihood to either end.
rows.curator_notes: The report names only a low and a high end rather than labelled cases. The share is against a forecast of 2028 national consumption, so it moves if national demand grows faster than assumed.

rows.source_name: Shehabi et al., "2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report", LBNL-2001637
rows.quote: the low and high end of roughly 325 and 580 TWh in 2028
rows.caveat: Excludes cryptocurrency mining and grid losses. The high end assumes GPU shipments at the top of the modelled range running near their rated power for most of the year; the report treats it as a bound, not an expectation.
rows.curator_notes: The report adds that at an assumed 50% capacity utilisation this range is 74-132 GW of power demand, which is how most utility restatements quote it.

rows.source_name: Shehabi et al., "United States Data Center Energy Usage Report" (2016), LBNL-1005775
rows.quote: data centers in the U.S. consumed an estimated 70 billion kWh
rows.caveat: Superseded: the same team's 2024 report revised 2014 down to about 58 TWh after updated shipment data, a changed definition of data center space types and lower assumed power for high-end servers. Excludes cryptocurrency mining and grid losses.
rows.curator_notes: Kept deliberately so the page can show how the published estimate of a fixed historical year moved. The 2024 report devotes a section to explaining the revision.

rows.source_name: Shehabi et al., "United States Data Center Energy Usage Report" (2016), LBNL-1005775
rows.quote: data centers are projected to consume approximately 73 billion kWh in 2020
rows.caveat: Badly superseded and kept as a record of how flat the view was before AI. This case assumed efficiency gains would keep consumption nearly level; the 2024 report says none of the 2016 scenarios captured the rise of AI. Excludes cryptocurrency mining.
rows.curator_notes: The 2016 report ran four further efficiency cases (improved management, best practices, hyperscale shift, and combinations) worth up to 33 billion kWh of savings by 2020, but prints no per-case 2020 level, so no rows for them.

rows.source_name: EPA, "Report to Congress on Server and Data Center Energy Efficiency, Public Law 109-431"
rows.quote: sector consumed about 61 billion kilowatt-hours (kWh) in 2006
rows.caveat: Covers servers, storage, networking and the power and cooling infrastructure that supports them, which the report puts at half the total. Pre-dates cryptocurrency mining entirely, and excludes grid losses.
rows.curator_notes: The oldest congressionally mandated US estimate and the ancestor of the Berkeley Lab series. Includes a federal-government subset of about 6 billion kWh.

rows.source_name: EPA, "Report to Congress on Server and Data Center Energy Efficiency, Public Law 109-431"
rows.quote: electricity use is expected to rise to about 107 billion kWh
rows.caveat: Superseded and far too high: later work put actual 2011 US data center use nearer 70 TWh, because virtualisation and the shift to hyperscale facilities cut consumption in ways this case did not foresee. Excludes cryptocurrency mining and grid losses.
rows.curator_notes: The baseline case of the 2007 report, carrying forward the efficiency trends visible at the time. Kept as the clearest example in this literature of a forecast that missed high.

rows.source_name: EPA, "Report to Congress on Server and Data Center Energy Efficiency, Public Law 109-431"
rows.quote: historical trends scenario is estimated at about 125 billion kWh
rows.caveat: A deliberate counterfactual rather than a forecast: it extrapolates 2000-2006 trends assuming no further efficiency improvement, so it is the report's upper bound and not what EPA expected. Excludes cryptocurrency mining and grid losses.
rows.curator_notes: Included because the gap between this case and the current-efficiency-trends case is how the report measured the value of efficiency already under way.

rows.source_name: EPRI, "Powering Intelligence: Analyzing Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Energy Consumption" (2024 white paper, 3002028905)
rows.quote: versus an estimated 4% today
rows.caveat: Cryptocurrency mining is explicitly excluded from this study, as are the grid losses upstream of the meter. The underlying quantity is an average 2023 data center load of about 152 TWh, well below Berkeley Lab's 176 TWh for the same year on a similar scope.
rows.curator_notes: Recorded as a share because the white paper states the 2023 position as a percentage in prose; the 152.1 TWh figure appears only in Table 3 as 152,120,846 MWh and is quoted in the caveat rather than as this row's value.

rows.source_name: EPRI, "Powering Intelligence: Analyzing Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Energy Consumption" (2024 white paper, 3002028905)
rows.quote: the graph shows the projection at a mid-range of 196.3 TWh/yr
rows.caveat: Excludes cryptocurrency mining by design and excludes grid losses. This case applies a 3.7% annual load growth rate to a 2023 base, and its share assumes all other US load grows at 1% a year, so the percentage moves if the rest of the economy grows faster.
rows.curator_notes: Built from data sources surveyed as of November 2023, which is why every case in this vintage now reads low against what was actually built.

rows.source_name: EPRI, "Powering Intelligence: Analyzing Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Energy Consumption" (2024 white paper, 3002028905)
rows.quote: moderate growth 5% scenario, the projection predicts a mid-range of 214.0 TWh/yr
rows.caveat: Excludes cryptocurrency mining and grid losses. A 5% annual load growth case; the share of national electricity assumes non-data-center load grows at 1% a year.
rows.curator_notes: EPRI's own 2026 update says this whole 2024 family of scenarios was about 60% too low.

rows.source_name: EPRI, "Powering Intelligence: Analyzing Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Energy Consumption" (2024 white paper, 3002028905)
rows.quote: data center energy usage rises to a mid-range of 296.4 TWh/yr
rows.caveat: Excludes cryptocurrency mining and grid losses. A 10% annual load growth case; the share of national electricity assumes non-data-center load grows at 1% a year.
rows.curator_notes: EPRI describes each case value as a mid-range of a bounding analysis, not a point forecast.

rows.source_name: EPRI, "Powering Intelligence: Analyzing Artificial Intelligence and Data Center Energy Consumption" (2024 white paper, 3002028905)
rows.quote: data center electricity usage rising to an average of 403.9 TWh/year
rows.caveat: Excludes cryptocurrency mining and grid losses. The 15% annual growth case, and the one behind the widely repeated headline that data centers could reach 9% of US electricity by 2030; it was the top of EPRI's 2024 range, not its central view.
rows.curator_notes: This is the number most press coverage of the 2024 white paper quoted, usually without the scenario label.

rows.source_name: EPRI, "Powering Intelligence: Updated U.S. Data Center Scenarios" (brief on the 2026 white paper)
rows.quote: In 2024, total U.S. data center electricity use is estimated at 177-192 TWh
rows.caveat: The low end of the 177-192 TWh range EPRI publishes for 2024. Unlike EPRI's 2024 white paper and Berkeley Lab's series, these estimates include cryptocurrency mining alongside small- and large-scale data centers, which is part of why they sit above Berkeley Lab's 176 TWh for 2023.
rows.curator_notes: Built from state-level operational capacity, construction in progress and announced plans rather than chip shipments. The brief PDF carries an early-March 2026 document date; the study was announced on 2026-02-26, which is the date recorded here.

rows.source_name: EPRI, "Powering Intelligence: Updated U.S. Data Center Scenarios" (brief on the 2026 white paper)
rows.quote: In 2024, total U.S. data center electricity use is estimated at 177-192 TWh
rows.caveat: The high end of the 177-192 TWh range EPRI publishes for 2024. Includes cryptocurrency mining as well as small- and large-scale data centers, so it is on a wider scope than Berkeley Lab's or EPRI's own 2024 figures. Excludes grid losses.
rows.curator_notes: Recorded as its own row rather than merged with the low end, so nothing on the page has to pick a midpoint.

rows.source_name: EPRI, "Powering Intelligence: Updated U.S. Data Center Scenarios" (brief on the 2026 white paper)
rows.quote: growing to roughly 380-790 TWh by 2030
rows.caveat: Includes cryptocurrency mining, which EPRI's 2024 white paper excluded, so the jump against the earlier vintage is partly scope and mostly real development. The low case assumes most projects under construction plus about a quarter of those in advanced planning become operational; announced capacity is treated as a pipeline indicator, not a firm forecast.
rows.curator_notes: Low end of the published 380-790 TWh range and of the 9%-17% share range. EPRI says the revised range is roughly consistent through 2028 with Berkeley Lab's December 2024 report despite a completely different method.

rows.source_name: EPRI, "Powering Intelligence: Updated U.S. Data Center Scenarios" (brief on the 2026 white paper)
rows.quote: growing to roughly 380-790 TWh by 2030
rows.caveat: Includes cryptocurrency mining. The high case assumes projects in early planning also get built; EPRI cautions that announced nominal capacity should be read as a pipeline indicator rather than a near-term peak forecast, because ramp-up, on-site generation and load flexibility all cut into the realised figure.
rows.curator_notes: High end of the 380-790 TWh range and of the 9%-17% share range. About 60% above EPRI's 2024 projections, driven by the development record of the preceding 18 months.

rows.source_name: IEA, "Energy and AI", chapter on energy demand from AI
rows.quote: Consumption increases by around 240 TWh (up 130%) in the United States
rows.caveat: This is growth on top of the 2024 US level, not a total, and must never be added to a level from another row. The IEA counts all data centres including those used for cryptocurrency mining, and measures electricity delivered to the site, excluding grid losses.
rows.curator_notes: The US figure sits inside a global report, which is why it is easy to misread as global. The corresponding global Base Case rows are recorded separately and labelled global.

rows.source_name: IEA, "Energy and AI", executive summary
rows.quote: around 1.5% of the world's electricity consumption in 2024, or 415 terawatt-hours
rows.caveat: A world total, not a US one: the IEA puts the US at 45% of it. Quoting this figure as American is the commonest error in this literature. The 1.5% is a share of world electricity, so it is not comparable with the US share columns elsewhere in this table.
rows.curator_notes: Kept mainly as the denominator that makes the IEA's US increment interpretable.

rows.source_name: IEA, "Energy and AI", executive summary
rows.quote: Data centre electricity consumption is set to more than double to around 945 TWh
rows.caveat: A world total, not a US one. The IEA also runs Lift-Off, High Efficiency and Headwinds sensitivity cases which diverge mainly after 2030, so this Base Case figure is not the only IEA number in circulation for that year.
rows.curator_notes: Recorded so a reader who meets 945 TWh in the press can see immediately that it is global.

rows.source_name: EIA, "Data center server energy use grows across the commercial building stock" (Today in Energy, on AEO2026)
rows.quote: reaches between 446 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) and 818 billion BkWh
rows.caveat: Servers only. Cooling, ventilation, power conversion and every other piece of data center infrastructure are outside this number, so it is roughly the IT-equipment share of what other rows in this table call data center consumption, and is not comparable with them. This case also assumes servers get 10% more efficient every three years after 2040.
rows.curator_notes: EIA meters the commercial sector rather than data centers, so even its own outlook reaches the subset only through a modelled end use. AEO2026 was released 2026-04-08 and reflects laws as of December 2025.

rows.source_name: EIA, "Data center server energy use grows across the commercial building stock" (Today in Energy, on AEO2026)
rows.quote: reaches between 446 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) and 818 billion BkWh
rows.caveat: Servers only, excluding cooling and other infrastructure, so it understates whole-facility consumption on the definition most other rows here use. EIA separately puts space cooling in this case 84 BkWh above the baseline in 2050, which gives a sense of what is left out.
rows.curator_notes: This case makes no assumption of post-2040 server efficiency gains and assumes AI servers take a larger share of the installed stock. Of the 818 BkWh, 581 BkWh is in standalone data centers.

rows.source_name: Goldman Sachs, "AI is poised to drive 160% increase in data center power demand"
rows.quote: Data centers will use 8% of US power by 2030, compared with 3%
rows.caveat: A rounded share with no TWh published alongside it and no statement of whether cryptocurrency mining is inside or outside the definition. The free article summarises three underlying reports whose methods and scope are not public.
rows.curator_notes: Recorded as a share because that is the only form the free article gives for the US.

rows.source_name: Goldman Sachs, "AI is poised to drive 160% increase in data center power demand"
rows.quote: Data centers will use 8% of US power by 2030, compared with 3%
rows.caveat: A single rounded share with no range and no TWh, and the article does not say whether cryptocurrency mining counts. The 160% growth figure in the headline is global, not American, and the two are often conflated.
rows.curator_notes: The article publishes one unnamed central estimate rather than named cases, so this row is labelled base. Companion figures: US power demand up 2.4% a year 2022-2030, of which about 0.9 points is data centers.

rows.source_name: Goldman Sachs, "US Data Center Power Demand Projected to Double by 2027"
rows.quote: US data center power demand is expected to climb from 31 gigawatts (GW)
rows.caveat: Power in gigawatts, not annual energy, and derived from an assumed 70% capacity utilisation applied to installed capacity rather than measured. Do not compare it with a TWh row without converting. Built on a commercial facility-level dataset whose coverage is not public.
rows.curator_notes: Goldman's commodities team, using Aterio activation data. Realised capacity additions were 6.4 GW in 2024 and 8.5 GW in 2025 on this basis.

rows.source_name: Goldman Sachs, "US Data Center Power Demand Projected to Double by 2027"
rows.quote: to 41 GW in 2026 and 66 GW the year after
rows.caveat: Power in gigawatts, not annual energy. It already discounts announced schedules, assuming only about 50-60% of capacity planned for the next one to two years arrives on time. The related 8.5% figure Goldman quotes for 2027 is a share of peak summer demand, not of annual consumption.
rows.curator_notes: The article publishes one adjusted forecast rather than named cases, so this row is labelled base. Implies roughly 95 GW of US capacity by end-2027 at 70% utilisation.

rows.source_name: Grid Strategies, "Power Demand Forecasts Revised Up for Third Year Running, Led by Data Centers"
rows.quote: roughly 90 GW are linked to data centers
rows.caveat: Growth in peak demand in gigawatts, not annual energy, and growth on top of 2025 rather than a total. It is what utilities filed on FERC Form 714, so it counts requested and planned load, and Grid Strategies itself judges the data center portion overstated by about 25 GW because not every announced project completes.
rows.curator_notes: The data center share of a 166 GW five-year national peak growth forecast, about 55% of it. Few utilities separate cryptocurrency mining from other data center load, so it is inside this figure where filers did not break it out.

rows.source_name: Grid Strategies, "Strategic Industries Surging: Driving US Power Demand"
rows.quote: aggregate utility data center load forecasts may exceed 90 GW
rows.caveat: Peak demand growth in gigawatts on top of 2024, not annual energy and not a total. Drawn from utility filings, which record requested load rather than signed contracts; the same report notes industry specialists put five-year data center growth anywhere from 10 GW to 65 GW.
rows.curator_notes: Kept alongside the 2025 edition so the page shows the same aggregation one year apart: the national five-year peak growth forecast moved from 128 GW to 166 GW while the data center component stayed near 90 GW.

rows.source_name: Deloitte, "As generative AI asks for more power, data centers seek more reliable, cleaner energy solutions" (TMT Predictions 2025)
rows.quote: data centers are anticipated to represent 6% (or 260 TWh) of total electricity consumption
rows.caveat: A single unnamed estimate with no range, and the piece does not state whether cryptocurrency mining is inside the definition. Most of the surrounding article is global, so the 1,065 TWh figure often quoted from it is a world total and not this one.
rows.curator_notes: Recorded as base because the article publishes one central figure rather than named cases. Useful as a near-term checkpoint: it is a 2024-vintage view of a year that has now largely happened.

rows.source_name: Deloitte, "Can US infrastructure keep up with the AI economy?"
rows.quote: reaching 123 gigawatts, up from 4 gigawatts in 2024
rows.caveat: AI data centers only, not all data centers, and power in gigawatts rather than annual energy, so it belongs beside none of the TWh rows without conversion and a scope adjustment. Cryptocurrency mining is outside it by definition.
rows.curator_notes: The AI subset is the fastest-moving part of the estimate and the part most sensitive to chip supply. Recorded as base because Deloitte publishes one estimate rather than named cases.

rows.source_name: BCG, "Breaking Barriers to Data Center Growth"
rows.quote: expected to total roughly 130 GW in 2028
rows.caveat: A world figure, not a US one, and power in gigawatts rather than annual energy. BCG's US statement in the same piece is that data centers account for up to 60% of total US load growth from 2023 to 2030, which is a share of growth and not a share of consumption.
rows.curator_notes: Recorded as base because BCG publishes one central path rather than named cases. Kept as a global anchor against which the US rows can be sized; BCG's widely repeated 2.5%-to-7.5% US share numbers come from a 2024 deck that is not reachable free on BCG's own site.
